questions.question: Surfactant replacement protects a preterm baby against all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Surfactant reduces RDS severity, air leaks (pneumothorax) and mortality. It does not protect against pulmonary haemorrhage, which is a recognised complication of surfactant. Its effect on IVH is neutral, so read the exact recalled wording.

questions.question: A baby of a diabetic mother is jittery and the bedside glucose is 2.3 mmol/L. What is your action?
questions.exp: A symptomatic (jittery) hypoglycaemic baby needs a confirmed lab glucose and IV dextrose (2 mL/kg 10% bolus then infusion) in the neonatal unit. Feeding and recheck is only for asymptomatic babies with mild hypoglycaemia.
questions.b: Encourage breastfeeding and recheck the glucose
questions.c: Admit to NICU, send a lab glucose and start IV dextrose

questions.question: A mother develops varicella 2 days before delivery. The membranes rupture the next day, she gets antibiotics and delivers. What should the baby receive?
questions.exp: Maternal varicella from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery exposes the baby before maternal IgG has crossed: give VZIG (or IVIG) as soon as possible and treat with IV aciclovir if lesions appear. Many units also give prophylactic aciclovir.
questions.a: Nothing; the baby is protected by maternal antibody
questions.c: VZIG, and aciclovir if the baby develops lesions

questions.question: A mother with Graves' disease has a TRAb of 25 at 28 weeks' gestation. What should be done for the baby?
questions.exp: High maternal TRAb in the third trimester puts the baby at risk of neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Check cord TRAb and TFTs at 3–5 days and 10–14 days, as maternal antithyroid drugs wear off; treat if hyperthyroid.
questions.a: Cord blood TRAb and thyroid function tests at day 3–5 (and again at 10–14 days)
questions.c: Observe and treat only if symptoms appear

questions.question: A preterm baby who had a long period of ventilation in NICU now has stridor. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Prolonged endotracheal intubation in preterm infants causes acquired subglottic stenosis, presenting with biphasic stridor weeks to months later. Assess by laryngobronchoscopy.

questions.question: A 26-week preterm baby on CPAP develops green aspirates, abdominal distension and bloody stools. Abdominal X-ray shows intramural (transmural) air; the chest is clear. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall) with distension and bloody stool is diagnostic of NEC (Bell stage II). Free air under the diaphragm would mean perforation.

questions.question: What is the most important risk factor for necrotising enterocolitis?
questions.exp: Prematurity is the strongest risk factor, followed by formula feeding, growth restriction with absent end-diastolic flow, and hypoxic-ischaemic insults. Breast milk is protective.

questions.question: A 3-month-old has a heart rate of 240 that responds to adenosine. The ECG afterwards shows a short PR interval with narrow QRS. What is the next step?
questions.exp: SVT in an infant with pre-excitation (WPW): do an echocardiogram to look for structural disease (e.g. Ebstein anomaly) and start prophylaxis such as propranolol. Ablation is deferred until the child is older (usually over 15 kg) unless refractory.

questions.question: A neonate has confirmed sensorineural hearing loss on otoacoustic emissions and a QT interval of 680 ms. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Congenital deafness with long QT = Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome (autosomal recessive, KCNQ1/KCNE1). Romano–Ward has normal hearing.

questions.question: A neonate has been resuscitated successfully after an arrest but is still unconscious. Blood glucose is 0.1 mmol/L. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Treat profound hypoglycaemia immediately with IV 10% dextrose bolus and maintenance infusion; recheck in 15–30 minutes. Secure the airway if needed, but the glucose is the reversible cause here.
questions.c: IV dextrose (10% 2–2.5 mL/kg) followed by an infusion

questions.question: A child with diabetes has DKA: capillary refill 4 s, glucose 11 mmol/L, pH 7.15 and potassium 6 mmol/L. What is the right order of treatment?
questions.exp: BSPED 2021: 10 mL/kg bolus in DKA with poor perfusion (20 mL/kg only in shock). Insulin infusion (0.05–0.1 U/kg/h) starts 1–2 hours after fluids. Potassium is added to fluids once K is below 5.5 mmol/L and the child passes urine, so with K 6 it is held and rechecked. The recall keyed 20 mL/kg + saline + insulin then KCl.
questions.a: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus, then saline and insulin, then potassium when K falls into range
questions.b: 0.9% saline 10 mL/kg bolus, then 0.9% saline with potassium, then insulin
questions.d: 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus, then saline with potassium, then insulin

questions.question: A 50 kg child in DKA has a capillary refill time over 3 seconds. How much fluid do you give immediately?
questions.exp: BSPED: 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 15 minutes for DKA that is not shocked, 20 mL/kg for shock; the maximum single bolus is 1 litre. The recall keyed 20 mL/kg (maximum 1 L).

questions.question: A teenager is in DKA with shock. How is the fluid deficit replaced?
questions.exp: BSPED 2021: deficit (weight × % × 10) is replaced evenly over 48 hours plus maintenance; initial boluses are subtracted only in children who were NOT shocked. In shock, boluses are not subtracted.

questions.question: An 18 kg child has 7% burns. Using the Parkland formula, how much fluid is needed in the first 24 hours?
questions.exp: Parkland: 4 mL × weight (kg) × %TBSA = 4 × 18 × 7 = 504 mL over 24 hours (half in the first 8 hours), plus maintenance. Formal resuscitation usually starts at 10% TBSA in children.

questions.question: A teenager with newly diagnosed diabetes presents with DKA after missing insulin doses; she is not interested in her treatment. What do you do?
questions.exp: Engage the young person directly, explain the risks and that her safety means involving parents and the diabetes MDT (including psychology). Missed insulin in a minor is a safety issue that can justify sharing information.
questions.a: Talk to her about her health and that you will involve her family and the diabetes team
questions.c: Tell the family without telling her

questions.question: A child with diabetes has DKA; the parents are divorced. What is the most important step?
questions.exp: Children moving between two households are at risk of missed insulin and inconsistent care. Both parents should be trained and communicate with the diabetes team.
questions.a: Ensure good communication between both parents and the diabetes team after discharge

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl with menarche at 13 has had no periods for a year. She has acne, hirsutism, acanthosis nigricans and BMI 25. Height is on the 2nd centile. Which test is LEAST useful?
questions.exp: Work-up of secondary amenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism: pregnancy test first, then testosterone (PCOS), 17-OHP (non-classic CAH), TFT and prolactin. LH:FSH ratio is no longer a diagnostic criterion for PCOS. The recall was uncertain; short stature also prompts thought of Cushing.

questions.question: An obese girl is worried about rough, dark skin at the back of her neck. What do you do?
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans marks insulin resistance; screen for type 2 diabetes and dyslipidaemia, then lifestyle change ± metformin. It fades with weight loss, but screening comes first.
questions.a: Check HbA1c (or OGTT), then dietary counselling; medication may be needed
questions.c: Reassure that it will vanish when she loses weight

questions.question: A child treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy for craniopharyngioma now has short stature, fatigue and a chest infection. Blood count and electrolytes are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Craniopharyngioma and cranial radiotherapy commonly cause hypopituitarism: GH deficiency (short stature), ACTH deficiency (fatigue, poor stress response) and TSH deficiency. Check pituitary function.

questions.question: A child treated with chemotherapy and cranial radiotherapy for a brain tumour 3 years ago now has short stature. What do you tell the parents?
questions.exp: GH deficiency is the earliest and commonest endocrine effect of cranial irradiation. Test pituitary function and replace hormones; MRI surveillance continues separately.
questions.a: It is a recurrence of the tumour
questions.b: It is most likely due to the treatment; we will do pituitary function tests and give hormone replacement as needed
questions.c: Growth hormone cannot be given after a brain tumour
questions.d: It is constitutional and needs no tests

questions.question: After treatment for a brain tumour, a child has height on the 2nd centile, weight on the 10th, low-normal IGF-1 and low cortisol. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Low cortisol and IGF-1 after cranial tumour therapy suggest hypopituitarism: perform dynamic pituitary testing and start hydrocortisone cover first.

questions.question: A mother has Huntington disease. The father wants his healthy children tested. What do you do?
questions.exp: Predictive testing for adult-onset conditions without treatment is deferred until the child can give informed consent (usually adulthood), protecting the child's autonomy and right not to know.
questions.a: Defer predictive testing until the children can decide for themselves
questions.c: Ask the young children whether they want it

questions.question: A mother with a symptomatic chromosome 4p deletion has a child. What is the chance that the child is affected?
questions.exp: A heterozygous deletion behaves like an autosomal dominant trait: each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the deleted chromosome.

questions.question: After an RTA a child has a head injury, GCS below 8, HR 40 and BP 120/85. What do you do?
questions.exp: GCS ≤8 needs intubation. Bradycardia with hypertension is a Cushing response: give hyperosmolar therapy, keep PaCO2 4.5–5.3 kPa (hypercapnia raises ICP) and get CT within 1 hour (NICE).
questions.a: Intubate with permissive hypercapnia and mannitol
questions.b: Head up 30° and mannitol, CT within 1 hour, no airway intervention
questions.c: Intubate, ventilate to normocapnia, give mannitol or 3% saline and CT within 1 hour
questions.d: Head up 30° and 3% saline, CT within 7 hours

questions.question: An infant has seizures due to hypocalcaemia, VSD and truncus arteriosus on echo, and recurrent infection. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: CATCH-22: cardiac defects (conotruncal), abnormal face, thymic hypoplasia (infections), cleft palate, hypocalcaemia (hypoparathyroidism).

questions.question: A girl has short stature (0.4th centile) and falling school performance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Short stature in a girl is Turner syndrome until proven otherwise; specific learning difficulties (visuospatial, maths) are common. Do a karyotype.

questions.question: A boy has poor school performance and a long face with a prominent jaw. His mother and her brother both left school early. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fragile X (FMR1 CGG repeat, X-linked): learning disability, long face, large ears and jaw, macro-orchidism after puberty; carrier females may have milder learning problems.

questions.question: A child has bloody diarrhoea, then pallor, jaundice and raised creatinine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: STEC-HUS (E. coli O157): microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI after bloody diarrhoea. Avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs.

questions.question: A child has a facial rash and arthritis. Hb and platelets are low, ANA is positive and the direct Coombs test is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Malar rash, arthritis, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and positive ANA meet SLE criteria.

questions.question: A child with dermatomyositis has a high CK. Which investigation best assesses the muscle involvement non-invasively?
questions.exp: Juvenile DM with typical rash and raised enzymes: MRI (T2/STIR) shows muscle oedema and guides biopsy if needed. Muscle biopsy is the gold standard when the diagnosis is uncertain. The recall listed biopsy and MRI.

questions.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome has abdominal pain and tenderness, generalised oedema, albumin 10 g/L, BP 100/50 and normal heart rate. What do you give?
questions.exp: Abdominal pain in nephrotic syndrome suggests spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (pneumococcus): IV ceftriaxone. Albumin is given for symptomatic hypovolaemia (20% 0.5–1 g/kg; 4.5% 10–20 mL/kg if shocked). Check local guidance.
questions.b: 4.5% albumin 20 mL/kg over 1 hour and antibiotics
questions.c: IV antibiotics (for possible peritonitis) and 20% albumin with furosemide if needed

questions.question: Which skin finding is NOT a feature of IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura)?
questions.exp: HSP rash starts urticarial/maculopapular and becomes palpable purpura and petechiae over the legs and buttocks. Splinter haemorrhages suggest infective endocarditis.

questions.question: What laboratory finding is expected in nephrotic syndrome?
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria (UPCR >200 mg/mmol), albumin <25 g/L, oedema and hyperlipidaemia (raised cholesterol and triglycerides).

questions.question: A child with nephrotic syndrome in relapse on prednisolone has contact with varicella and is not immune. What do you give?
questions.exp: Immunosuppressed, non-immune contacts get VZIG within 10 days (or oral aciclovir from day 7). Live varicella vaccine waits until at least 1 month off high-dose steroids.
questions.a: VZIG (or aciclovir prophylaxis) now; varicella vaccine later once off high-dose steroids

questions.question: A child on desmopressin has severe morning headaches for 2 weeks and blurred vision. What is the most likely problem?
questions.exp: Morning headache with blurred vision is a red flag for raised intracranial pressure; in a child on desmopressin also check sodium for water intoxication. The recall options (NSAIDs, dexamethasone, pizotifen, triptan) were unclear, so this was rebuilt around the safe answer.
questions.c: Water intoxication (hyponatraemia) from desmopressin, or raised ICP needing urgent assessment

questions.question: A girl is over-tidy, arranges pencils by colour and washes her hands after touching food. Development and communication are normal and she does well at school. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Repetitive compulsions (ordering, washing) driven by anxiety with normal social communication suggest OCD; first-line treatment is CBT with exposure and response prevention.

questions.question: A boy with ADHD on treatment shows impulsive, agitated behaviour and stealing. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.exp: Conduct problems in ADHD respond to parent-training programmes and behavioural therapy; review medication dose only after assessing adherence and comorbidity.

questions.question: A child on haloperidol develops fever, rigidity, reduced dark/red urine and raised creatinine. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Antipsychotics can cause NMS (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, high CK) with myoglobinuric AKI. Stop the drug, cool, hydrate, and consider dantrolene or bromocriptine. The recall's options were status dystonicus, UTI, convulsions.

questions.question: Which is NOT a recognised association of coeliac disease?
questions.exp: Coeliac disease is associated with iron/folate deficiency, dermatitis herpetiformis, type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease and Addison disease (autoimmune). Hyposplenism can raise platelets, so the recall was uncertain; low cortisol (Addison) is an accepted association.

questions.question: Which histological feature is characteristic of ulcerative colitis?
questions.exp: UC: continuous mucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses and crypt distortion. Cobblestoning, skip lesions, transmural inflammation and granulomas are Crohn's disease.

questions.question: A girl has recurrent pneumonia, nystagmus and balance problems. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: AT (ATM gene): progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency (low IgA, IgG2) with sinopulmonary infections, raised AFP and cancer risk.

questions.question: An unimmunised child with sickle cell disease has fever and pallor. Which pairing is most likely?
questions.exp: Asplenic children with SCD are at risk of overwhelming sepsis from encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Hib). Low reticulocytes would suggest parvovirus aplastic crisis.
questions.c: Hb 7, high reticulocytes, Haemophilus influenzae / pneumococcus

questions.question: An infant has recurrent pneumonia, eczema herpeticum and a low platelet count. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: WAS (X-linked): eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets and recurrent infections. Cure is stem cell transplant.

questions.question: A child with asthma receives a blood transfusion after trauma and has an anaphylactic reaction. What is the likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.exp: Selective IgA deficiency patients may make anti-IgA antibodies and react to blood products; give IgA-deficient or washed products. It is associated with atopy and coeliac disease.

questions.question: A week after a URTI, a child has fever, seizures, slurred speech and weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: ADEM: post-infectious, polyfocal deficits with encephalopathy 1–3 weeks after infection; MRI shows multifocal white matter lesions. Treat with IV methylprednisolone.

questions.question: Which lymph node in a child is most significant?
questions.exp: Supraclavicular nodes are always abnormal and suggest malignancy (lymphoma) or TB; investigate urgently.

questions.question: A child has erythema migrans and arthritis from Lyme disease. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Lyme arthritis: oral doxycycline (≥8 years) or amoxicillin for 28 days; IV ceftriaxone only for persistent arthritis or neurological disease.
questions.a: Doxycycline with NSAID, review in 2 weeks
questions.b: Ceftriaxone with NSAID, review in 2 weeks
questions.d: Doxycycline (or amoxicillin) with NSAID, review in 4 weeks

questions.question: Which is NOT a feature of Perthes disease?
questions.exp: Perthes: painless or painful limp with groin, thigh or knee pain in a 4–8-year-old; the child is systemically well. Fever suggests septic arthritis or osteomyelitis.

questions.question: An athletic adolescent has leg pain on exercise. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Exercise-related tibial pain in a runner is usually medial tibial stress syndrome or a stress fracture; Baker cysts are popliteal swellings. (Recall options were partial.)
questions.b: Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) / tibial stress fracture

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has had pneumonia and Salmonella osteomyelitis. Which is NOT a feature of sickle cell disease?
questions.exp: SCD complications include dactylitis, haemolytic jaundice and gallstones, stroke, acute chest syndrome and splenic sequestration. HSV infection is not a feature.

questions.question: A girl has large café-au-lait patches that do not cross the midline and precocious puberty (McCune–Albright). Which is NOT a feature?
questions.exp: Axillary freckling is a feature of NF1. McCune–Albright: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait ('coast of Maine', respecting the midline) and endocrine hyperfunction.

questions.question: A child has cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and mediastinal nodes on X-ray. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Suspected lymphoma: excision biopsy of an accessible node gives the diagnosis. Check airway risk with a mediastinal mass before sedation. A full blood count and film first excludes leukaemia.

questions.question: A boy has posterior urethral valves. Which investigation is LEAST needed initially?
questions.exp: PUV is diagnosed with ultrasound and confirmed by MCUG; urine culture looks for infection. DMSA (scarring/differential function) comes later.

questions.question: Which is NOT a feature of concussion?
questions.exp: Concussion causes headache, confusion, amnesia, vomiting and dizziness without focal deficit. A cranial nerve palsy suggests structural injury (e.g. temporal bone fracture).

questions.question: A child with tricyclic antidepressant overdose has a broad QRS on ECG. What do you give?
questions.exp: Sodium bicarbonate (1–2 mmol/kg) narrows the QRS and prevents arrhythmia in TCA toxicity by alkalinisation and sodium loading.

questions.question: A tall boy has gynaecomastia and small testes. What is the karyotype?
questions.exp: Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY, tall, small firm testes, gynaecomastia, hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism and infertility.

questions.question: What is erythema chronicum migrans a sign of?
questions.exp: An expanding annular rash with central clearing at a tick bite site is the hallmark of early Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi).

questions.question: A child with G6PD deficiency and a UTI develops haemolysis. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Oxidant drugs trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency: sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole), nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, quinolones and naphthalene.

questions.question: Which of these bacteria is Gram-negative?
questions.exp: Pseudomonas is a Gram-negative rod. Staphylococci, streptococci and Listeria are Gram-positive.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa has bradycardia and hypotension. What do you do?
questions.exp: Admission criteria (MEED): HR below 40 (or 50), hypotension, postural changes, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance or rapid weight loss. Refeed cautiously with phosphate monitoring.
questions.c: Admit for medical stabilisation and supervised refeeding

questions.question: A child with enuresis has had behavioural therapy without success. What is the next step?
questions.exp: NICE: after reward systems, the alarm is first-line for motivated families; desmopressin when rapid short-term dryness is needed or the alarm is unsuitable. The recall wrote both.

questions.question: Which form of epidermolysis bullosa is autosomal dominant?
questions.exp: EB simplex (keratin 5/14) is mostly autosomal dominant; junctional EB is autosomal recessive. Dystrophic EB can be dominant or recessive. The recall wrote junctional with question marks.
